litigant

/LIT-ih-guhnt/ - the stress falls on LIT · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Litigant means someone engaged in a lawsuit.

The mediation service exists to keep neighbors from becoming litigants — cheaper, the flyer notes, to talk than to sue.

Example

For seven years Mrs. Okafor was a litigant against the railway over the orchard it had paved: she filed the suit the spring she turned sixty, answered every motion herself, and shook the company lawyer's hand when the settlement finally came.

Litigant covers exactly the people with a stake in the suit — the one who files and the one who answers. The lawyers argue it, the witnesses inform it, the jurors decide it; only the parties themselves are litigants.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

plaintiff: The plaintiff is only the side that files the suit — the party doing the complaining. Litigant covers both sides: the plaintiff who sues and the defendant who answers are each a litigant from the moment the case is docketed.

claimant: A claimant formally asserts a right or demand — to an inheritance, a payout, a benefit — and may press it entirely outside court. A litigant is defined by the lawsuit itself: until a case is actually filed and answered, there is no litigant.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

onlooker: watches the case with no stake in it

outsider: has no connection to the dispute at all

Where it sits · how close the quarrel is to court

grumbler → disputant → litigant

grumbler vs. litigant: A grumbler is far milder than a litigant — he mutters at the fence line and files nothing, while the litigant has already put the quarrel before a judge.

disputant vs. litigant: A disputant stops short of a litigant: the argument is real but still lives in letters and doorways; the litigant has carried it into court.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — litig: to go to law (Latin lis, lawsuit + agere, to drive)

Suffix — -ant: one who

Put it together: Litig- (to go to law — Latin lis, 'lawsuit,' plus agere, 'to drive') + -ant (one who) = one who drives a lawsuit. The -ant works as it does in contestant or applicant: it names the person doing the thing.

Use the root in a new word: litigation: The startup set aside a quarter of its budget for litigation.

Word Choice

legal

Litigant is courtroom vocabulary for the parties themselves — whoever is suing or being sued. The lawyers, witnesses, and jurors around them are not litigants. Outside legal contexts, plainer words like 'the two sides' carry the load.
